interest: Written in late July 1941, just days after the United States froze Japanese assets in response to the occupation of southern Indochina, this document provides valuable ground-level insight into the rapid liquidation of American commercial enterprises in Japan immediately preceding the Pacific War. It illustrates the direct coercive involvement of local Japanese police authorities in labor disputes, functioning as advocates for Japanese employees to extract substantial severance settlements from withdrawing foreign firms. Additionally, it highlights the structural friction between American corporate compensation models—higher base pay without retirement benefits—and Japanese expectations of customary dismissal allowances, enforced by wartime state intervention.
overview: This file consists of a single two-page consular despatch dated July 31, 1941, from American Consul Gerald Warner in Kobe, Japan, addressed to Secretary of State Cordell Hull regarding the resolution of retirement allowance disputes involving Japanese staff at the Kobe branch of the States Steamship Company. Following protracted negotiations involving branch manager Robert McClelland, local employees, and Japanese police authorities, a compromise severance agreement was reached granting workers one month's average salary per year of service plus August pay. With commercial maritime operations no longer viable under mounting geopolitical tensions and economic restrictions, McClelland advised the firm's immediate closure, while Consul Warner observed that police mediation was routinely compelling foreign firms in Kobe to grant generous termination allowances of up to two months' salary per year of service.

subfiles.about: Report on the settlement of retirement allowance disputes for Japanese staff of the States Steamship Company in Kobe and the manager's recommendation to close the office.
subfiles.summary: American Consul Gerald Warner reports on the compromise settlement of retirement allowance claims brought by local Japanese personnel against the Kobe branch of the States Steamship Company. Mediated through multiple conferences involving branch manager Robert McClelland, the employees, and local Japanese police authorities, the agreement established a severance payout of one month's average salary per year of service plus compensation for August 1941. Concluding that business had become impossible under prevailing conditions, McClelland formally recommended the immediate liquidation and closure of the Kobe office. Warner adds that Japanese police were systematically intervening across the consular district to enforce severance payouts of up to two months' salary per year of service for dismissed staff of foreign firms.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Gerald Warner (Kobe) on Settlement of Retirement Allowance Difficulties of the States Steamship Company
